semantic_correction.stem: A child arrives with high fever, drooling, inspiratory stridor, a muffled voice, and a tripod position. The nurse suspects epiglottitis. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Keep the child upright and calm, avoid examining the throat, and activate the team for controlled emergency airway management.
options.B: Place the child supine for a complete throat examination and use a tongue depressor to look for epiglottic swelling.
options.C: Send the child for a lateral neck radiograph before calling the airway team so the diagnosis can be confirmed first.
options.D: Start an intravenous line and collect throat and blood cultures before escalating care because treatment depends on the results.

semantic_correction.rationale: Pediatric epiglottitis is a life-threatening upper-airway emergency. Current NCBI/StatPearls guidance describes drooling, stridor, distress and tripod positioning as classic pediatric findings and emphasizes that agitation, lying the child flat, unnecessary procedures, and oral/throat instrumentation can precipitate sudden airway compromise. The pediatric airway should be stabilized before diagnostic testing; a tongue depressor should not be used to examine the throat, and unstable children should not be sent to radiology before airway control. The safest nursing response is to keep the child upright and calm, minimize manipulation, and immediately activate experienced airway support for controlled emergency management. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan explicitly includes emergency care procedures and management of clients with impaired ventilation/oxygenation under Physiological Adaptation. Therefore A is the uniquely best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: When pediatric epiglottitis is suspected, minimize agitation and airway manipulation, keep the child in a position of comfort, and rapidly activate expert airway management rather than examining the throat or delaying for tests.
semantic_correction.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / StatPearls; National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.source_version_date: StatPearls Epiglottitis last updated October 5, 2024 and rechecked August 20, 2026; NCSBN Test Plan published 2025 and effective April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2029
semantic_correction.source_locator: NCBI StatPearls Epiglottitis > pediatric presentation/evaluation/management — drooling, stridor, tripod positioning; do not instrument the pediatric airway during oral examination; avoid supine positioning, agitation, unnecessary IV placement or radiology before airway stabilization; airway management is the priority. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan > Physiological Adaptation, printed p. 46 / PDF p. 50 — perform emergency care procedures, manage impaired ventilation/oxygenation, recognize complications and intervene.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: retired a CMS Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program item because it tested value-based purchasing policy rather than entry-level bedside nursing. Rebuilt the UID into a pediatric epiglottitis airway emergency requiring safe positioning, minimal manipulation and rapid expert airway escalation.

audit_findings_append.finding: The replacement tests a direct airway-safety decision. NCBI guidance supports minimizing agitation/manipulation and prioritizing controlled airway management in pediatric epiglottitis.

scope_exclusions.antibiotic_regimen: No antibiotic choice, dose, route, or treatment duration is tested; antimicrobial therapy follows airway stabilization and clinician orders.
scope_exclusions.intubation_technique: The nurse is not instructed to independently intubate the child or choose a specific airway device; the item requires rapid activation of experienced airway personnel.
scope_exclusions.radiographic_sign: No thumb-sign interpretation or imaging criterion is tested because imaging should not delay airway management in a clinically unstable child.
scope_exclusions.etiology: The item does not assume Haemophilus influenzae type b or another specific pathogen.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for 'epiglottitis drooling tripod tongue depressor airway child' returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank rescan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It minimizes airway-provoking manipulation and activates expert emergency airway management while allowing the child to remain upright and calm.
option_audit.B: Plausible diagnostic impulse, but supine positioning and tongue-depressor examination can precipitate airway collapse in suspected pediatric epiglottitis.
option_audit.C: Plausible because a lateral neck film can show epiglottic swelling in selected stable patients, but airway stabilization should not be delayed for imaging in this presentation.
option_audit.D: Plausible infection-workup response, but IV placement and cultures should not precede airway stabilization when manipulation may precipitate decompensation.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. B directly performs a dangerous throat examination, C delays airway management for imaging, and D delays/agitates the child for diagnostic procedures. A alone follows the source-supported pediatric airway priority.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. The correct option is not longest and all alternatives are realistic multi-step emergency actions.
